title: Beyond Traditional Strategy Execution — and Why It's Failing
author: Marc
summary: Marc dismantles the widely-cited claim that '70-90% of strategies fail,' tracing it to a single 1982 Fortune article and showing how it calcified into management folklore without empirical grounding. He argues the real failure mode is not execution in the traditional sense but a horizontal coordination gap: the inability of cross-functional teams to align day-to-day decisions with strategic intent. The article introduces a living strategy model in which execution is not a project managed from the top but a continuous behavioral output of how leaders at every level interpret, communicate, and prioritize. Marc identifies five leadership dimensions that determine whether a designed strategy becomes a lived one and critiques the assumption that better documentation or more review cadences will fix what is fundamentally a mobilization problem. He concludes that strategy failure is leadership failure, not planning failure.
points: The '70-90% of strategies fail' statistic is management folklore traced to a 1982 Fortune article — it lacks empirical grounding.
The real failure mode in strategy is a horizontal coordination gap: cross-functional teams cannot align their daily decisions with strategic intent.
Living a strategy requires mobilization — the ability to move people across functions toward shared priorities — not better documents or more review meetings.
Strategy execution fails not because the strategy was wrong but because it was never translated into daily leadership behavior across the organization.
Strategy failure is a leadership failure, not a planning failure — when leaders cannot connect their decisions to strategic intent, the strategy exists only on slides.
quotes: When McKinsey mapped what separates the organizations that pull away from the ones that don’t, across the arc of design → mobilize → execute, the widest capability gap was in mobilization — the work between deciding a strategy and doing it, the work that gets a strategy to survive its own organization’s inertia.

When two academics finally went looking for the empirical basis of the “60–90% fail” range — a proper literature audit — they concluded the estimates were “based on evidence that is outdated, fragmentary, fragile or just absent,” and that the true failure rate remains undetermined.

If strategies “mysteriously fail” at some spooky, ambient 80% rate, then the failure feels like weather — unpredictable, external, nobody’s fault — and the natural response is to go buy a tighter execution framework and cascade harder.

If this is the problem you recognize — a good strategy that never reached Monday morning, a review cadence that tells you everything except whether you’re still right — I’m teaching a live masterclass on closing exactly that gap.

You bring your own organization and one real strategy you’re trying to make live, and you diagnose — precisely — where it stops being lived, across the five leadership dimensions that turn a designed strategy into a lived one.

Trace it to its origin and the whole edifice rests on a single 1982 Fortune magazine article in which a consultant estimated that “fewer than 10% of effectively formulated strategies get successfully implemented.” That’s it.
They’re designed at the top, cascaded down, and absorbed by a business that’s already full — and the daily work simply carries on reproducing the old strategy, regardless of what was approved.
